title: Dot Product
body:
The **dot product** (inner product, scalar product) takes two [[Vector|vectors]] and returns a
**number**, not a vector. Multiply componentwise and add:

$$
\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = u_1v_1 + u_2v_2 + \cdots + u_nv_n = \sum_{i=1}^{n} u_iv_i
$$

In matrix notation, $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}^T\mathbf{v}$, a $(1 \times n)(n
\times 1)$ product giving a $1 \times 1$. That is not a coincidence: **every entry of a
[[Matrix Multiplication]] is a dot product**, of a row with a column. Learn this operation
properly and matrix multiplication stops being a rule to memorise.

## What it means

$$
\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|\cos\theta
$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between them. This is the identity that makes the dot product worth
having, because it says a componentwise sum secretly knows about angles. Rearranged, it is how
you *find* the angle:

$$
\cos\theta = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|}
$$

and since $\|\mathbf{u}\|$ and $\|\mathbf{v}\|$ are positive, the **sign of the dot product is
the sign of $\cos\theta$**:

| $\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}$ | Angle | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| $> 0$ | $\theta < 90°$ | pointing broadly the same way |
| $= 0$ | $\theta = 90°$ | **orthogonal** |
| $< 0$ | $\theta > 90°$ | pointing broadly opposite |

That middle row is the important one. **Orthogonality is defined as a dot product of zero**,
which extends "perpendicular" to $\mathbb{R}^n$ where you cannot draw the right angle. It also
extends past vectors entirely: two functions are orthogonal when their inner product (an
integral rather than a sum) is zero, which is the entire basis of Fourier series. See
[[Orthogonal Functions]] in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]].

Special case worth noting: $\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \|\mathbf{v}\|^2$, so the norm is the
square root of a vector dotted with itself.

## Properties

$$
\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}, \qquad
\mathbf{u} \cdot (\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}) = \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w},
\qquad
(c\mathbf{u}) \cdot \mathbf{v} = c(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})
$$

**Commutative**, unlike [[Matrix Multiplication]]. There is no associativity to state, because
$(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}) \cdot \mathbf{w}$ is not a legal expression: the left half is a
scalar.

The **Cauchy-Schwarz inequality** $|\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}| \leq
\|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|$ is what guarantees the $\cos\theta$ formula produces something in
$[-1, 1]$, so the angle exists at all.

## Projection

The **projection of $\mathbf{u}$ onto $\mathbf{v}$** is the part of $\mathbf{u}$ that lies along
$\mathbf{v}$: the shadow $\mathbf{u}$ casts on $\mathbf{v}$'s line.

$$
\text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2}\,\mathbf{v}
$$

Read it as two pieces: the fraction is *how much* (a scalar), and $\mathbf{v}$ is *which way*.
If $\mathbf{v}$ is a unit vector this collapses to $(\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v})\mathbf{v}$,
which is why normalising first is usually worth it.

What is left over, $\mathbf{u} - \text{proj}_{\mathbf{v}}\mathbf{u}$, is orthogonal to
$\mathbf{v}$. So any vector splits into a component along $\mathbf{v}$ and a component
perpendicular to it, uniquely. That decomposition is the engine behind
[[Orthonormal Basis|orthogonal bases]], [[Least Squares]], and [[Fourier Coefficients]], all of
which are the same move: **project onto each direction and keep the coefficients**.
[[Projection]] in [[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]] takes it from one vector to a whole
subspace, which is where the rest of that course starts.

## Where the degree uses it

- **A neuron computes a dot product.** The weighted sum $\sum w_ix_i$ of inputs against
  [[Weights]] is exactly $\mathbf{w} \cdot \mathbf{x}$, and then the
  [[Activation Function]] is applied to that one number. Stack the neurons of a layer and the
  dot products become one [[Matrix Multiplication]], which is what a [[Forward Pass]] is.
- **Similarity.** Cosine similarity between two vectors is the $\cos\theta$ formula and nothing
  more. It is the standard measure of how alike two documents or embeddings are, because it
  compares direction and ignores magnitude.
- **Work in physics** is force dotted with displacement, the original reason for the
  "how much of this is along that" reading.
- **[[Fourier Coefficients]]** are projections of a function onto $\sin$ and $\cos$, using the
  integral inner product.

## Related

- [[Basis]]: an orthonormal basis is one where all the pairwise dot products vanish, which makes
  finding coordinates a matter of projecting rather than solving
